import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 90: The unit distance problem

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/90](https://www.erdosproblems.com/90)

The conjecture asks whether every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determines at most
$n^{1 + O(1/\log\log n)}$ unit distances. It was **disproved** in May 2026: an internal model at
OpenAI produced a construction beating the conjectured bound, with the proof digested and
human-verified in two arXiv papers:

* W. Sawin, [*An explicit lower bound for the unit distance problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579)
  (2026), giving $u(n) \ge n^{1.014114}/C$ for infinitely many $n$;
* N. Alon, T. F. Bloom, W. T. Gowers, D. Litt, W. Sawin, A. Shankar, J. Tsimerman, V. Wang and
  M. Matchett Wood, [*Remarks on the disproof of the unit distance conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20695)
  (2026), giving the qualitative form $u(n) \ge n^{1+\varepsilon}$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$.

This file records the main statement (`erdos_90`), the two constructive disproof variants, the
logical implications between them, and the load-bearing reductions of Sawin's proof
(`sawin_lattice_reduction` and `sawin_totally_real_tower`) as further benchmark challenges.
-/

open Filter EuclideanGeometry NumberField
open scoped EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos90
open Finset

/--
The set of all possible numbers of unit distances for a configuration of $n$ points.
-/
noncomputable def unitDistanceCounts (n : ℕ) : Set ℕ :=
  {unitDistNum points | (points : Finset ℝ²) (_ : points.card = n)}

/--
This lemma confirms that the set of possible unit distance counts is bounded above, which
ensures that taking the supremum (`sSup`) is a well-defined operation. The trivial upper bound is
the total number of pairs of points, $\binom{n}{2}$.
-/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem unitDistanceCounts_BddAbove (n : ℕ) : BddAbove <| unitDistanceCounts n := by
  use n.choose 2
  rintro _ ⟨points, rfl, rfl⟩
  exact unitDistNum_le_choose_two points


/--
The **maximum number of unit distances** determined by any set of $n$ points in the plane.
This function is often denoted as $u(n)$ in combinatorics.
-/
noncomputable def maxUnitDistances (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  sSup (unitDistanceCounts n)


/--
Does every set of $n$ distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ contain at most
$n^{1+O(\frac{1}{\log\log n})}$ many pairs which are distance $1$ apart?

This was
[disproved](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/74c24085-19b0-4534-9c90-465b8e29ad73/unit-distance-proof.pdf)
by an internal model at OpenAI, which constructed (for infinitely many $n$) a set $P$ of $n$ points
in $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that the number of unit distance pairs in $P$ is at least $n^{1+c}$, where
$c > 0$ is an absolute constant.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_90 : answer(False) ↔ ∃ (O : ℕ → ℝ) (hO : O =O[atTop] (fun n => 1 / (n : ℝ).log.log)),
    (fun n => (maxUnitDistances n : ℝ)) =ᶠ[atTop] fun (n : ℕ) => (n : ℝ) ^ (1 + O n) := by
  sorry

/--
**Constructive form of the disproof.** There is an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that
infinitely many $n$ admit a configuration realising at least $n^{1+c}$ unit distances.

This is the qualitative content of Theorem 1.1 of Alon–Bloom–Gowers–Litt–Sawin–Shankar–
Tsimerman–Wang–Matchett Wood, [*Remarks on the disproof of the unit distance conjecture*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20695)
(2026). An explicit bound $c \ge 0.014114$ is given by Sawin, [*An explicit lower bound for the
unit distance problem*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579) (2026); see
`erdos_90.variants.sawin_explicit` below.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_90.variants.polynomial_lower_bound :
    ∃ c > (0 : ℝ),
      {n : ℕ | (n : ℝ) ^ (1 + c) ≤ (maxUnitDistances n : ℝ)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
**Sawin's explicit exponent.** The constructive disproof can be realised with $c \ge 0.014114$
(absorbing the implicit constant $C$ of Sawin's Theorem 1 into a slightly smaller exponent for
all large enough $n$). Reference: Theorem 1 of Sawin, [arXiv:2605.20579](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579)
(2026).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_90.variants.sawin_explicit :
    {n : ℕ | (n : ℝ) ^ (1.014114 : ℝ) ≤ (maxUnitDistances n : ℝ)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/-- Sawin's explicit bound implies the qualitative polynomial lower bound, by taking
$c = 0.014114$. -/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_90.variants.sawin_explicit_implies_polynomial_lower_bound :
    type_of% erdos_90.variants.sawin_explicit →
    type_of% erdos_90.variants.polynomial_lower_bound := by
  intro h
  exact ⟨0.014114, by norm_num, by convert h; norm_num⟩

/-- The polynomial lower bound implies the answer to Erdős 90 is `False`: a fixed positive
exponent $c$ is incompatible with the conjectured $O(1 / \log \log n)$ growth. -/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem erdos_90.variants.polynomial_lower_bound_implies_erdos_90 :
    type_of% erdos_90.variants.polynomial_lower_bound →
    type_of% erdos_90 := by
  rintro ⟨c, hc, hInf⟩
  refine ⟨fun h => h.elim, fun ⟨O_fn, hO_bigO, hO_eq⟩ => ?_⟩
  -- 1/log(log(n)) → 0, so O_fn = O(1/log log n) implies O_fn → 0
  have hg : Tendsto (fun n : ℕ => (1 : ℝ) / (↑n : ℝ).log.log) atTop (nhds 0) := by
    simp_rw [one_div]
    exact tendsto_inv_atTop_zero.comp
      (Real.tendsto_log_atTop.comp (Real.tendsto_log_atTop.comp tendsto_natCast_atTop_atTop))
  have hO_zero : Tendsto O_fn atTop (nhds 0) :=
    (Asymptotics.isLittleO_one_iff ℝ).mp
      (hO_bigO.trans_isLittleO ((Asymptotics.isLittleO_one_iff ℝ).mpr hg))
  -- Eventually u(n) < n^{1+c}, contradicting the infinitely-often lower bound
  have hLt : ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, ¬((n : ℝ) ^ (1 + c) ≤ (maxUnitDistances n : ℝ)) := by
    filter_upwards [hO_eq, hO_zero.eventually (Iio_mem_nhds hc), eventually_ge_atTop 2]
      with n hEq hOLt hn
    rw [not_le, hEq]
    exact Real.rpow_lt_rpow_of_exponent_lt (by exact_mod_cast (by omega : 1 < n)) (by linarith)
  rw [← cofinite_eq_atTop] at hLt
  exact hInf.frequently_cofinite hLt

/--
**Sawin's Lemma 2: lattice geometry of unit distances** (Sawin, [arXiv:2605.20579](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579)).

Let $d \ge 1$, $R \ge 2$, and suppose $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{R}^{2d}$ is a lattice equipped with
an additive embedding $\pi : \Lambda \to \mathbb{R}^2$. Suppose $S \subseteq \Lambda$ is a finite
set of "matching" vectors satisfying $\|v\| \le 1$ and $\|\pi v\| = 1$ for every $v \in S$. Then
there is a finite point set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with unit-distance density at least
$(1 - 1/R)^{2d}\,\#S$, i.e. $(1-1/R)^{2d}\,\#S\,\#U \le \#\{\text{unit pairs in } U\}$.

This pure geometry-of-numbers reduction is the elementary heart of the disproof.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem sawin_lattice_reduction
    (d : ℕ) (hd : 1 ≤ d) (R : ℝ) (hR : 2 ≤ R)
    (Λ : Submodule ℤ (EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (2*d))))
    (π : Λ →+ ℝ²) (hπ : Function.Injective π)
    (S : Finset Λ)
    (hS_norm : ∀ v ∈ S, ‖(v : EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin (2*d)))‖ ≤ 1)
    (hS_proj : ∀ v ∈ S, ‖π v‖ = 1) :
    ∃ U : Finset ℝ², 0 < U.card ∧
      ((1 : ℝ) - 1/R) ^ (2*d) * (S.card : ℝ) * (U.card : ℝ) ≤
        (unitDistNum U : ℝ) := by
  sorry

/--
**Sawin's Lemmas 11–12 / Remarks Proposition 2.3: the totally real tower.**

There exist $rdBound : \mathbb{R}$ and a *single* infinite set $Q$ of rational primes
$q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ such that for every $N$ one can find a totally real number field $F/\mathbb{Q}$
of degree $\ge N$ with bounded root discriminant $|disc F|^{1/[F:\mathbb{Q}]} \le rdBound$ in which
*every* prime $q \in Q$ splits completely.

The load-bearing feature is the quantifier order: $Q$ is fixed *before* $F$, so the same primes
split completely in fields of *unbounded* degree. (For a single fixed $F$, Chebotarev already
gives infinitely many completely split primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so a per-field statement would
be vacuous.) This uniform splitting in an unbounded tower is the key arithmetic input to the
disproof. It is proved as Lemmas 11–12 of Sawin, [arXiv:2605.20579](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579),
and as Proposition 2.3 of the [Remarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20695) paper, via the
Golod–Shafarevich inequality for pro-$2$ groups together with the Hajir–Maire–Ramakrishna (2003)
tower construction.

A "completely split" rational prime $q$ in $F$ is one for which $(q)$ is the product of exactly
$[F:\mathbb{Q}]$ distinct maximal ideals.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/n-yamaguchi-0729/SawinTotallyRealTowers/blob/3a455e1aa9140dbbe7b7d68f508392a69c86d0f4/Lean4/SawinTotallyRealTowers/SawinTotallyRealTower.lean#L31"]
theorem sawin_totally_real_tower :
    ∃ (rdBound : ℝ) (Q : Set ℕ), Q.Infinite ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime ∧ q % 4 = 1) ∧
      ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ (F : Type) (_ : Field F) (_ : CharZero F) (_ : NumberField F)
        (_ : IsTotallyReal F),
        N ≤ Module.finrank ℚ F ∧
        (|(NumberField.discr F : ℝ)|) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / Module.finrank ℚ F) ≤ rdBound ∧
        ∀ q ∈ Q, ∃ (factors : Finset (Ideal (𝓞 F))),
          factors.card = Module.finrank ℚ F ∧
          ∀ p ∈ factors, p.IsMaximal ∧ (q : 𝓞 F) ∈ p := by
  sorry

end Erdos90

findings.description: The conclusion omits the quantitative upper bound on `U.card`, and the statement has no shortest-vector parameter. Sawin's Lemma 2 simultaneously controls the size and unit-distance density of U; the size bound is essential for turning the density into a polynomial lower bound in the number of points. Here U can be arbitrarily large and unrelated to the lattice parameters. Consequently, the conclusion follows from the elementary fact that planar unit-distance density is unbounded, without using any of the lattice hypotheses: choose k unit vectors with distinct subset sums; their 2^k subset sums determine at least k·2^(k−1) unit pairs, giving density at least k/2. This density-only assertion does not state the cited quantitative reduction.
findings.source_evidence: Sawin, arXiv:2605.20579v1, Lemma 2 (`set-from-lattice`), defines ρ as the minimum norm of a nonzero lattice vector and states BOTH `#U ≤ (2R/ρ + 1)^(2d)` and the ordered-unit-pair density bound `(1−1/R)^(2d) M`. Proposition 10 explicitly uses this upper bound on #U to obtain its exponent. The original OpenAI proof likewise explains in §2.2 that a uniform size bound is needed to turn the geometric construction into a bound in n. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579 and the cited unit-distance-proof.pdf.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the simultaneous size and density bounds. Require an actual lattice, and introduce ρ > 0 equal to, or a lower bound for, the norm of every nonzero lattice vector. The conclusion should include `(U.card : ℝ) ≤ (2 * R / ρ + 1) ^ (2*d)`. In this quantitative formulation, convert Sawin's ordered-pair count correctly: the density inequality should have `2 * (unitDistNum U : ℝ)` on the right. For the full Lemma 2 rather than its Euclidean-norm specialization, also allow an arbitrary ambient norm and R > 1.

findings.description: The docstring incorrectly attributes the fixed infinite set of completely split rational primes to Sawin's Lemmas 11–12 and dates the Hajir–Maire–Ramakrishna construction to 2003. Sawin's cited lemmas concern a finite prescribed prime set and inertia degrees at most 2; they do not state this infinite completely-split-prime result. The other citation, Remarks Proposition 2.3, does support the declaration, so the mathematics need not change.
findings.source_evidence: Sawin, arXiv:2605.20579v1, Lemmas 11–12 (`group-infinite`, `field-existence`), explicitly use a finite set S_Q and conclude bounded inertia. Alon et al., arXiv:2605.20695v1, Proposition 2.3 states the infinite totally real tower with infinitely many completely split primes q ≡ 1 mod 4. Its bibliography identifies Hajir–Maire–Ramakrishna, Cutting towers of number fields, Annales Mathématiques du Québec 45 (2021), 321–345, not 2003.
findings.suggested_fix: Attribute this infinite-Q formulation to Remarks Proposition 2.3 and the 2021 Cutting towers of number fields paper. Remove the claim that it is the statement of Sawin's Lemmas 11–12, or describe those separately as related finite-prime, bounded-inertia reductions.

reformulations.difference: Lean uses eventual equality `u(n) = n^(1 + O(n))` with an existential Big-O error function, whereas the source asks for an eventual upper bound on every n-point configuration.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n ≥ 4, u(n) ≥ n, as witnessed by a unit square extended by a unit-length chain. Given the source upper bound, set O(n) = log(u(n))/log(n) − 1; eventually 0 ≤ O(n) ≤ C/log log n and the equality holds. Conversely, the Big-O norm bound on O gives the source upper bound because exponentiation with base n > 1 is increasing. The maximum is attained, so bounding it is equivalent to bounding every configuration. Both the geometric lower bound and the complete equivalence, including the False polarity, were proved without sorry in /workspace/review/final_checks.lean.

reformulations.difference: Complete splitting is expressed by the existence of [F:ℚ] distinct maximal ideals containing q, without explicitly asserting that their product is the ideal (q).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a rational prime q in a degree-n number field, the fundamental identity is Σ_{p|q} e_p f_p = n, with every e_p and f_p a positive integer. A Finset of n distinct maximal ideals containing q therefore exhausts the primes above q, and all ramification indices and residue degrees equal 1. Consequently (q) is exactly their product and q splits completely. Conversely, complete splitting supplies precisely such a Finset. The primality hypothesis on every q ∈ Q and the positive finite field degree ensure this characterization applies.

reformulations.difference: The Remarks theorem uses a sequence of configurations whose cardinalities tend to infinity; Lean uses an infinite set of natural-number sizes satisfying a bound on the maximum.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An infinite subset of ℕ is unbounded and admits a strictly increasing enumeration. For each enumerated size, choose a configuration attaining maxUnitDistances, whose attainment was checked in Lean. This gives the source's sequence with the same fixed positive exponent. Conversely, a sequence with cardinalities tending to infinity yields infinitely many qualifying sizes, since each configuration's count is bounded by the maximum. Including n = 0 adds only one possible exception and does not affect infinitude.

review.notes: No defect was found in sawin_explicit: although Theorem 1's rounded headline retains a constant, its proof and Proposition 10 give δ = 0.0141144286784982… by numerical evaluation of the stated formula. This is strictly larger than 0.014114, so both the fixed constant and the ordered/unordered factor 2 can be absorbed while retaining Lean's exponent. A general constant-absorption lemma was proved in Lean. Other checks established nonempty count sets, attainment of the maximum, u(0)=u(1)=0, u(2)=1, and only standard axioms for the three existing proved tests. The linked external tower theorem matches the target; its source dependency scan found no sorry or custom axioms. I did not rebuild that 1,600-module Lean 4.33.0 project or independently run #print axioms on its final theorem. All mathematical declarations were checked; the external rebuild is a proof-audit limitation, not an unresolved statement-faithfulness issue.

not_demonstrated.reason: The missing size bound weakens the quantitative theorem, but the resulting statement is neither false nor a logical tautology. An unconditional proof still requires constructing planar configurations with unbounded unit-distance density and proving the associated pair count. I found no existing sorry-free lemma making this a handful-line proof. The earlier scratch argument assumes unbounded density, so it does not demonstrate the declaration itself; invoking the admitted lower-bound theorems would also be inappropriate.

submission.summary: No trivial_proof.lean file was created. This finding does not admit the requested short, honest demonstration using the available API.
submission.gave_up_reason: Proving the weakened declaration requires genuine geometric and combinatorial arguments, beyond the permitted trivial-proof scope. A conditional proof or an unrelated non-lattice example would not demonstrate the reported missing quantitative conclusion.

not_fixed.reason: Left the previously reported minor bibliographic issue unchanged; this patch is limited to the requested lattice statement.

submission.summary: Restored the simultaneous point-count and density bounds, with genuine-lattice hypotheses and a positive separation lower bound ρ. Generalized the ambient space to an arbitrary 2d-dimensional normed real space, allowed R > 1, corrected the ordered/unordered counting factor, and updated the docstring. Compilation reports only the permitted sorry warnings.

      (hO_bigO.trans_isLittleO ((Asymptotics.isLittleO_one_iff ℝ).mpr hg))
  -- Eventually u(n) < n^{1+c}, contradicting the infinitely-often lower bound
  have hLt : ∀ᶠ (n : ℕ) in atTop, ¬((n : ℝ) ^ (1 + c) ≤ (maxUnitDistances n : ℝ)) := by
    filter_upwards [hO_eq, hO_zero.eventually (Iio_mem_nhds hc), eventually_ge_atTop 2]
      with n hEq hOLt hn
    rw [not_le, hEq]
    exact Real.rpow_lt_rpow_of_exponent_lt (by exact_mod_cast (by omega : 1 < n)) (by linarith)
  rw [← cofinite_eq_atTop] at hLt
  exact hInf.frequently_cofinite hLt

**Sawin's Lemma 2: lattice geometry of unit distances** (Sawin, [arXiv:2605.20579](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579)).

Let $d \ge 1$ and let $E$ be a $2d$-dimensional normed real vector space, whose norm need not
be Euclidean. Suppose $\Lambda \subset E$ is a full-rank lattice equipped with an additive
embedding $\pi : \Lambda \to \mathbb{R}^2$, and $\rho > 0$ is a lower bound for the norms of its
nonzero vectors. Suppose $S \subseteq \Lambda$ is a finite set of "matching" vectors satisfying
$\|v\| \le 1$ and $\|\pi v\| = 1$ for every $v \in S$, where the norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ is Euclidean.
Then for every $R > 1$ there is a nonempty finite point set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ such that
$$
\#U \le (2R/\rho + 1)^{2d}, \qquad
(1 - 1/R)^{2d}\,\#S\,\#U \le 2\nu(U),
$$
where $\nu(U)$ is the number of unordered unit-distance pairs in $U$. The factor $2$ converts
`unitDistNum` to the ordered-pair count used by Sawin.
-/

**Sawin's Lemmas 11–12 / Remarks Proposition 2.3: the totally real tower.**

There exist $rdBound : \mathbb{R}$ and a *single* infinite set $Q$ of rational primes
$q \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ such that for every $N$ one can find a totally real number field $F/\mathbb{Q}$
of degree $\ge N$ with bounded root discriminant $|disc F|^{1/[F:\mathbb{Q}]} \le rdBound$ in which
*every* prime $q \in Q$ splits completely.

The load-bearing feature is the quantifier order: $Q$ is fixed *before* $F$, so the same primes
split completely in fields of *unbounded* degree. (For a single fixed $F$, Chebotarev already
gives infinitely many completely split primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$, so a per-field statement would
be vacuous.) This uniform splitting in an unbounded tower is the key arithmetic input to the
disproof. It is proved as Lemmas 11–12 of Sawin, [arXiv:2605.20579](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20579),
and as Proposition 2.3 of the [Remarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20695) paper, via the
Golod–Shafarevich inequality for pro-$2$ groups together with the Hajir–Maire–Ramakrishna (2003)
tower construction.

A "completely split" rational prime $q$ in $F$ is one for which $(q)$ is the product of exactly
$[F:\mathbb{Q}]$ distinct maximal ideals.
-/

theorem sawin_totally_real_tower :
    ∃ (rdBound : ℝ) (Q : Set ℕ), Q.Infinite ∧ (∀ q ∈ Q, q.Prime ∧ q % 4 = 1) ∧
      ∀ N : ℕ, ∃ (F : Type) (_ : Field F) (_ : CharZero F) (_ : NumberField F)
        (_ : IsTotallyReal F),
        N ≤ Module.finrank ℚ F ∧
        (|(NumberField.discr F : ℝ)|) ^ ((1 : ℝ) / Module.finrank ℚ F) ≤ rdBound ∧
        ∀ q ∈ Q, ∃ (factors : Finset (Ideal (𝓞 F))),
          factors.card = Module.finrank ℚ F ∧
          ∀ p ∈ factors, p.IsMaximal ∧ (q : 𝓞 F) ∈ p := by
